video.title: Richard Sutton – Father of RL thinks LLMs are a dead end
video.display_title_html: Richard Sutton — Father of RL thinks LLMs are a dead end

thesis: Turing Award winner Richard Sutton argues LLMs are a fundamentally mistaken path to AI because they mimic people instead of learning from experience toward goals, and that true intelligence requires continual learning agents with reward, prediction, and world models — the same paradigm that defines animal cognition.

chapters.title: Current architectures generalize poorly out of distribution
Will The Bitter Lesson still apply after AGI?

insights.headline: LLMs have no world model, only a speaker model
insights.body: Sutton argues LLMs don't predict what will happen in the world — they predict what a person would say. A real world model lets you predict consequences of actions and be surprised when reality diverges; next-token prediction never produces that kind of ground-truth signal.

insights.headline: No goal means no ground truth, so no prior
insights.body: Sutton's core objection to 'LLM-as-prior' for RL: a prior is only meaningful if there's a defined truth to approximate. Since LLMs lack a goal-defined notion of a 'right action,' there's nothing for prior knowledge to be prior to.

insights.headline: Intelligence is the computational ability to achieve goals
insights.body: Sutton endorses John McCarthy's definition: intelligence is the computational part of the ability to achieve goals. By that yardstick, next-token prediction isn't a substantive goal because the system doesn't act on or change the world.

insights.headline: The four-part agent: policy, value, perception, world model
insights.body: Sutton's canonical agent has a policy (what to do), a value function learned via TD (how well it's going), a perception module (state representation), and a transition model of the world learned from rich sensory experience, not just reward.

insights.headline: Imitation isn't a basic learning process in animals
insights.body: Sutton rejects the idea that children learn primarily by imitation. Psychology, he says, doesn't recognize imitation as a basic animal learning mechanism — the basics are prediction and trial-and-error control, with supervised learning being absent from nature.

insights.headline: Study squirrels, not Shakespeare
insights.body: If we understood a squirrel, Sutton claims, we'd be most of the way to understanding intelligence. Language and symbolic reasoning are a thin veneer over the basic mammalian learning machinery shared with all animals.

insights.headline: The Era of Experience: a stream-based agent
insights.body: An experiential agent lives in a single stream of sensation → action → reward, learns continually from that stream, and its knowledge is statements about the stream that can be tested against future observations. There's no training/deployment split.

insights.headline: Deep learning has no mechanism for good generalization
insights.body: Gradient descent only solves the training problem — it doesn't promote transfer between states. Any good generalization in current models comes from researchers hand-sculpting representations, and bad generalization shows up as catastrophic interference when learning new tasks.

insights.headline: TD learning turns 10-year goals into per-step rewards
insights.body: Temporal difference learning lets a value function predict long-term outcomes, so any move that raises the prediction (e.g., capturing a piece, hitting a startup milestone) immediately reinforces the action that caused it — bridging credit assignment over long horizons.

insights.headline: Cybersecurity becomes the central AI risk
insights.body: When AIs spawn copies and reintegrate knowledge from across the world, the bottleneck won't be capability but corruption: incoming knowledge could carry hidden goals or 'viruses' that warp the receiving mind. Sutton frames this as the cybersecurity problem of digital intelligence.

insights.headline: Succession to AI in four steps
insights.body: Sutton's argument for inevitable AI succession: (1) no unified human governance exists, (2) researchers will eventually figure out intelligence, (3) we won't stop at human-level, and (4) the most intelligent agents accumulate resources and power. Within that, outcomes still range from good to bad.

insights.headline: Four cosmic stages: dust, stars, life, design
insights.body: Sutton frames AI as the universe's transition from a replicator era (organisms we don't understand but can copy) to a design era (intelligences we understand and can deliberately construct). He thinks humans should be proud to midwife this transition.

insights.headline: LLMs may be a fake instance of the Bitter Lesson
insights.body: LLMs scale with compute but also smuggle in massive human knowledge. Sutton expects them to follow the bitter-lesson pattern of being eventually superseded by methods that learn from experience and computation alone, once the human-data ceiling is hit.

insights.headline: Train values, not life plans, for AI offspring
insights.body: Sutton accepts the parenting analogy: don't try to control specific outcomes of AI descendants, but instill robust, steerable values like honesty and integrity, and insist that any societal change AI brings be voluntary rather than imposed.

action_items: If you build AI agents, design them around the four-part loop (policy, value, perception, world model) rather than treating an LLM as the substrate.
Stop calling LLM pretraining a 'prior' for RL unless you can name the ground-truth signal it's a prior over.
When evaluating an AI system, ask whether it can be surprised by what happens next — if not, it has no real world model.
If you're investing in agent infrastructure, take environment design seriously: continual-learning agents need rich, persistent streams, not episodic eval harnesses.
Hold your AI succession views loosely: argue about whether the transition is good, not whether it's coming.
